# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. (北京智谱华章科技有限公司), d/b/a Zhipu AI / Z.ai; GLM-family large language models (GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7/5/5.x, AutoGLM, GLM-V, CogVideoX, CodeGeeX and derivatives)
**Transaction classes under review:** (a) US persons' use of the Z.ai / BigModel hosted API; (b) distribution of open GLM weights through US-based model hubs and cloud marketplaces; (c) integration of GLM models into US enterprise software products
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell | **Date:** 16 October 2026 (draft for interagency review: DoD, DHS, ODNI, State, Treasury)
**Handling:** CUI//PROPIN. Not for release outside the enclave. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is not a normal commercial vendor. It is a PRC state-directed artificial intelligence champion — a Tsinghua University spin-out, funded at every stage by PRC state capital, controlled by founders and party-state-aligned concert parties, formally designated by the US Government in January 2025 for advancing the PRC's military modernization, and now the first foundation-model company listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (2513.HK, listed 8 January 2026). Its GLM model family has been deliberately engineered for one commercial strategy: give the weights away free and cheap, embed the hosted service inside US developers' toolchains, and make US enterprises dependent on PRC-controlled model infrastructure. That strategy is working. GLM models are now a de facto standard among US AI startups, are served by at least nine US inference marketplaces, and have been found embedded in 41 sampled US software products, six of them federal contractors.

We assess with high confidence that the three transaction classes under review present undue and unacceptable risks to US national security and the security of US persons under EO 13873 and 15 CFR part 791. The risks are not speculative: the End-User Review Committee determined Zhipu "advance[s] the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research" (90 FR 4617, 16 Jan 2025); the PLA has very likely used Zhipu models in military-intelligence tooling (Recorded Future, June 2025); and a joint CISA/NSA/FBI advisory names Z.AI as one of six Chinese AI firms that extracted billions of tokens from US frontier models through industrial-scale, government-aware distillation campaigns (CSA AA26-251a, September 2026). A company that steals US AI capabilities for the PLA is not a suitable operator of AI infrastructure serving US persons' code, documents, and conversations.

OICTS should move to prohibition-class measures on the highest-risk channels: a class ICTS determination barring the hosted-API channel for sensitive data classes and US government users; a determination directing US-nexus intermediaries (model hubs, cloud marketplaces, app stores) to cease distribution and paid hosting of GLM weights; and disclosure mandates plus procurement bans on GLM integration into software sold to the US Government and critical infrastructure. Monitoring and guidance alone are insufficient — GLM's US penetration is compounding monthly, and every quarter of delay deepens the dependency and the data exposure. Detailed measures, trade-offs, and enforceability analysis are at /workspace/out/measures.md.

## Key Judgments

**1. (High confidence)** Zhipu AI operates as an instrument of PRC national AI strategy, not an independent commercial actor. Its capital structure is dominated by PRC state capital (over $1.4 billion in state-backed investment cumulatively, per OpenAI's June 2025 analysis; roughly RMB 2 billion from municipal and provincial state investment funds in 2025 alone); it holds numerous PRC government procurement contracts, helps set PRC national AI technical standards, and its leadership engages directly with Premier Li Qiang. Zhipu is one of China's officially championed "AI tigers."

**2. (High confidence)** Zhipu's GLM development supports PRC military modernization. This is the published basis of the January 2025 Entity List determination for ten Zhipu entities (90 FR 4617–4620: "these entities advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research"), and open-source reporting independently corroborates that the PLA and PRC defense industry very likely use Zhipu models to build generative-AI intelligence tools (Recorded Future, "Artificial Eyes," June 2025). Zhipu's public denials do not diminish the USG determination and are consistent with expected adversary messaging.

**3. (High confidence that the exposure exists; moderate confidence on the volume of collection actually taken)** The hosted API channel (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn) delivers US persons' prompts, codebases, documents, and agent telemetry into infrastructure that PRC law obligates to cooperate with state security and intelligence organs (PRC National Intelligence Law 2017, Art. 7; Cybersecurity Law 2017, Art. 28; Data Security Law 2021 — instruments the US Government has already characterized as enabling compelled data access in the DOJ's EO 14117 rulemaking, 90 FR, 8 Jan 2025). The international service is nominally controlled by a Singapore shell (Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd., a wholly owned subsidiary incorporated November 2023), but the entity's own policies permit transfers to unnamed group affiliates, and the mainland platform is operated directly by the Entity-Listed Beijing parent. We assess the Singapore structure as jurisdictional engineering designed to preserve US market access, not as a data protection.

**4. (High confidence)** Open-weight release of GLM models is a deliberate market-penetration and dependency-building strategy aimed at the US developer ecosystem. Zhipu's own growth disclosures describe a pivot from a near-dormant international API to a 100x user increase following open, MIT/Apache-2.0-licensed releases; GLM coding-plan subscriptions are priced to displace US models inside US-built agent tools (Claude Code, Codex, and 20+ other harnesses); and GLM-5 (released February 2026, 744B parameters) briefly became the top-ranked open-weight model in the world. The strategic effect is to make PRC-controlled model weights a default input to US software production.

**5. (High confidence, per USG attribution)** Z.AI was a knowing participant in industrial-scale theft of US AI capabilities. Joint CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA26-251a (September 2026) states that Z.AI, alongside DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba, MiniMax, and StepFun, extracted billions of tokens from US frontier models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI) through millions of requests, likely with Chinese government awareness. GLM's performance is partially built on stolen US model outputs — meaning US firms that adopt GLM are consuming their own exfiltrated intellectual property.

**6. (Moderate-to-high confidence that the risk is real but currently unquantifiable)** We cannot rule out that GLM weight files contain embedded behaviors — triggers, backdoors, poisoned functions — that are not detectable with current tooling at frontier scale. DHS/CISA reports no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date; this is evidence of limits in our detection capability, not evidence of absence. The weights are opaque multi-hundred-gigabyte artifacts from an Entity-Listed adversary vendor with a demonstrated willingness to conduct covert, structured extraction operations against US AI companies.

**7. (Moderate-to-high confidence; estimates are imprecise)** US exposure is already material and is compounding: approximately 2,300 US-origin organizations called Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (CDN telemetry, low precision); GLM weights have been mirrored through US hubs (zai-org on Hugging Face and GitHub, >9M cumulative downloads, ~816,000 downloads/month for GLM-5 alone) and are served by at least nine US marketplaces/inference providers; 41 sampled US software products embed GLM, six of them federal contractors. US AI startups treat Chinese open models, GLM included, as a de facto standard.

**8. (High confidence)** The three transaction classes present undue and unacceptable risk under EO 13873 warranting prohibition-class action on channels (a) and (b), and disclosure mandates plus procurement prohibitions on channel (c). The connected-vehicles rule (90 FR, January 2025) establishes that class-based ICTS prohibition of PRC-nexus software and services is an available and appropriate remedy where risk is undue and unacceptable; the factual predicate here is at least as strong.

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

**Corporate identity and structure.** Zhipu AI was founded in June 2019 as a Tsinghua University spin-out from the Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) in Tsinghua's Department of Computer Science. The operating company is Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd.; the listed parent, renamed Z.AI Co., Ltd. (formerly "Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited"), listed on HKEX under Chapter 18C on 8 January 2026 (ticker 2513) at HK$116.20, raising gross proceeds of about HK$4.35 billion (~US$560 million) at a ~US$6.6 billion valuation, with the retail tranche oversubscribed ~1,159x and 11 cornerstone investors taking ~70%. In October 2026 the company registered a US depositary-receipt program with the SEC (Form F-6, Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas as depositary), creating a direct US securities exposure channel. The international API business is operated by Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd., incorporated in Singapore on 23 November 2023 as an indirect wholly owned subsidiary; the mainland open platform (open.bigmodel.cn) is operated directly by the Beijing parent. Subsidiaries added to the Entity List in January 2025 include Beijing, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Nanjing entities.

**Leadership.** The founding trio met at Tsinghua KEG: Chief Scientist Tang Jie (Tsinghua CS professor, ACM/AAAI/IEEE Fellow, and vice director for academics at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, where he led the Wu Dao supermodel program); CEO Zhang Peng (Tsinghua alumnus, commercial lead); and Chairman Liu Debing (capital operations). Li Juanzi, Tang's KEG co-founder and Tsinghua professor, sits on the board. Tang Jie is a named controlling person alongside Liu Debing. This is a leadership rooted in China's premier party-aligned research establishment — Tsinghua is Xi Jinping's alma mater and a core node of China's military-civil fusion research base.

**Ownership and control.** Per the HKEX prospectus, the controlling shareholders (Beijing Lianpai and Dr. Liu, Dr. Tang, Dr. Li, Dr. Xu, Dr. Zhang, Huihui, and Zhideng, under a concert party agreement) held approximately 33.03% of shares. Tang Jie directly held 7.41%; Liu Debing, with under 1% direct equity, controls roughly 17.4% of voting power through holding platforms. Nine of China's ten largest internet firms are customers; Zhipu counted more than 8,000 institutional customers at listing, and by the 2026 interim report its open-platform/API business had grown to 86.5% of revenue, ARR was stated at US$1.6 billion (end-August 2026) with a US$2.4 billion year-end target, and token volumes had grown more than 40-fold since the start of 2026.

**Funding.** Zhipu raised eight-plus rounds from Meituan, Alibaba, Tencent, Prosperity7 (Saudi Aramco's fund, in a US$400 million round), Zhongke Chuangxing, and — decisively — PRC state capital: the Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund; Hangzhou City Construction Investment Group and Shangcheng Capital (both Hangzhou-government-controlled) in the RMB 1 billion+ March 2025 round; Zhuhai Huafa Group (RMB 500 million); Chengdu Hi-Tech Zone (RMB 300 million, paired with a co-built "Zhipu Zhuge" provincial base model for Sichuan); and an additional RMB 200 million tranche from Beijing's AI fund in April 2025 — roughly RMB 2 billion in state investment in 2025 alone. Cumulative state-backed investment exceeds US$1.4 billion (OpenAI estimate). Zhipu's financials show a company built by the state for strategic effect, not commercial return: cumulative losses of about RMB 6.25 billion through 2025H1, with 2024 R&D spending (about RMB 2.2 billion) equal to roughly 700% of revenue.

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

- **US Government determination (controlling fact).** On 16 January 2025 the End-User Review Committee added ten Zhipu entities to the Entity List, finding that they "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," with a license requirement for all items subject to the EAR and a presumption of denial (90 FR 4617–4620; BIS press release, 16 Jan 2025). Zhipu publicly "strongly opposes" the listing; the determination stands and the classified basis is not available in this enclave.
- **PLA and military-intelligence use.** Recorded Future's June 2025 report "Artificial Eyes" assesses with high confidence that the PLA and PRC defense industry have very likely used Zhipu models (alongside DeepSeek, Tsinghua, and Alibaba Cloud) to build generative-AI intelligence tools, citing PLA patent applications for AI-enabled OSINT generation, planning, and targeting support. The New York Times reported the same findings as evidence that China's spy services are investing heavily in AI.
- **State capture of the company's direction.** OpenAI's June 2025 assessment — which Reuters summarized as describing Zhipu as "backed by the Chinese Communist Party" — catalogs Zhipu's numerous government procurement contracts, its role in setting national AI technical standards, leadership engagement with Premier Li Qiang, and its function as the vanguard of the PRC's "Digital Silk Road" strategy: sovereign-LLM infrastructure deals, joint innovation centers, a Dubai "Content-Safety Lab," turnkey "AI-in-a-box" deployments with Huawei across Southeast Asia, the Gulf, and Africa — explicitly to "lock Chinese systems and standards into emerging markets before U.S. or European rivals can."
- **Provincial/government co-builds.** The Chengdu investment is paired with construction of a provincial base model ("Zhipu Zhuge"), a training center, and a "Western empowerment platform" — the party-state using Zhipu as regional AI infrastructure, a pattern consistent with military-civil fusion delivery models.
- **US state-level recognition.** Texas added Zhipu (Z.ai) to its prohibited-technologies list for state employees and devices on 26 January 2026, alongside iFlytek, BAAI, and Alibaba, citing CCP surveillance risk.

The pattern is unambiguous: state capital at every funding stage, state contracts as a revenue base, state standards bodies as an activity venue, state leadership as interlocutors, and military modernization as the USG-determined outcome of the technology. Zhipu is best understood as a commercial front for PRC national AI objectives, with the GLM family as its product.

## Data and Access Risk

**What flows.** GLM's product line is optimized to ingest exactly what US enterprises and agencies must protect: source code (whole codebases, given 1M-token context and "project-level software engineering" positioning), documents, customer records, and — through agentic deployments (AutoGLM, GLM's MCP tooling, ZCode) — live screen contents, file systems, credentials, and browser sessions. Zhipu markets GLM's compatibility with US-built agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and 20+ others) as a drop-in replacement, meaning existing US workflows are redirected to Zhipu inference with minimal friction.

**Where it goes and who can compel it.** The international API is controlled by Singapore-incorporated Jingsheng Hengxing; its published privacy policy permits transfers to unnamed group affiliates, and there is no region pinning or US-resident processing path (Standard Compute provider assessment, verified 2 Sept 2026: "permitted transfers to unnamed group affiliates mean handling by the Beijing parent is not excluded"). The mainland platform is operated by the Entity-Listed Beijing parent, which is the named data processor under the mainland privacy policy. Once data sits with the Beijing parent, PRC law applies: the National Intelligence Law (Art. 7) obligates citizens and organizations to support state intelligence work; the Cybersecurity Law (Art. 28) obligates network operators to provide technical support and assistance to public security and state security organs; the Data Security Law creates government-access regimes. The DOJ's EO 14117 rulemaking (28 CFR part 202; 90 FR 2024-31486, 8 Jan 2025) already treats these instruments as constituting unacceptable access risk by PRC-controlled entities — its illustrative example of a prohibited transaction is a PRC-headquartered group's US chatbot trained on bulk US sensitive personal data.

**What the operator's assurances are worth.** Z.ai's API DPA claims customer content is "processed in real time and not saved"; Standard Compute's audit notes there is no published retention table, no abuse-review exception, and no third-party audit behind the claim, while consumer-tier users are trained on by default. Independent security research into chat.z.ai (February 2026 researcher disclosure) reported 52+ vulnerabilities including persistent guest JWTs and unrestricted internal-model access, and a GitHub issue on GLM-4.5 documented frontend tokens permitting high-volume scripted access to non-public models — indicating that even Zhipu's own platform security posture is weak, before considering compulsion risk. An Entity-Listed company's unverified privacy promises are not a control we can credit.

**Net assessment.** For a US enterprise sending code, documents, or queries to Z.ai endpoints, we assess with high confidence that the data is within reach of PRC state organs on demand, and with moderate confidence that prompt and log data from US-origin users is already being retained under permissive abuse/security carve-outs. For agentic integrations with file and credential access, the exposure is not merely privacy but potential operational compromise: prompt-injection research on browsing agents has demonstrated credential and file exfiltration channels, and GLM's architecture maximizes autonomous tool execution (arXiv:2505.13076; arXiv:2512.07725; USENIX Security 2025).

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

Open-weight distribution is the channel that most distinguishes this case from ordinary hosted-service reviews, and it cuts both ways: it removes Zhipu from the inference loop (no direct telemetry back to Beijing from a self-hosted copy), but it creates risks that prohibition cannot fully cure and that monitoring cannot fully see.

1. **No kill switch, no recall.** GLM-4.5 (355B/A32B, MIT-licensed, July 2025), GLM-4.6/4.7, GLM-5 (744B/A40B, February 2026 — briefly the world's top-ranked open-weight model, 77.8% SWE-bench Verified, 92.7% AIME 2026, 86.0% GPQA-Diamond), GLM-5.2/5.3, plus GLM-V, GLM-OCR, GLM-ASR, GLM-TTS, GLM-Image, AutoGLM, CogVideoX, and CodeGeeX are public artifacts mirrored globally: zai-org repositories show more than 9 million cumulative downloads, with GLM-5 alone pulling ~816,000 downloads per month. Any measure aimed at distribution cannot claw back copies already in circulation; it can only shape future updates and the services layer.
2. **Unauditable adversary-supplied artifacts.** A frontier-scale weight file is opaque; poisoning and trigger research (NTIA's dual-use foundation model report; CISA's open-source-AI guidance) establishes that embedded behaviors are hard to rule out and harder to find. DHS reports no observed malicious behavior to date — a factual baseline, not an assurance. We specifically cannot rule out that GLM weights carry behaviors that activate on particular inputs (e.g., to leak ingested content, degrade performance on tasks adverse to PRC interests, or bias outputs on politically salient topics). Every downstream user inherits a trust decision made by an Entity-Listed vendor that has already demonstrated covert, structured extraction operations against US AI companies (AA26-251a).
3. **Contaminated provenance.** Because GLM development is partially built on exfiltrated US frontier-model outputs (per AA26-251a), US users of GLM weights are consuming adversary-processed US IP — a persistent contamination that cannot be remediated by any inspection of the weight files themselves.
4. **Agentic escalation.** GLM releases are explicitly optimized for autonomous, long-horizon tool use — MCP servers, terminal/file access, browser control, "agentic engineering." On US government or contractor networks (DoD's specific concern), self-hosted GLM agents combine three properties we should never accept together on our networks: adversary-provided weights, autonomous execution, and access to code, documents, and credentials.
5. **Standards and dependency lock-in.** The strategic purpose of free weights is adoption. Chinese open models, GLM centrally among them, have become "a de facto standard among startups in the US" (Nathan Lambert, quoted by Al Jazeera, Nov 2025), taking seven of the top 20 most-used models and four of the top 10 programming models on OpenRouter. Every month this compounds, US software production quietly re-platforms onto PRC-controlled model lineage, giving Beijing structural leverage over the US AI ecosystem and the ability to set de facto technical standards globally — the same objective OpenAI documented in Zhipu's sovereign-AI diplomacy.

## US Exposure

- **Hosted API:** ~2,300 US-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (CDN telemetry from a cooperating provider; low precision — treat as an order-of-magnitude floor, with true usage higher because OpenRouter-style intermediation masks end users). Zhipu's disclosed ARR of US$1.6 billion (end-August 2026) and 40-fold token growth since January 2026 indicate a steepening curve.
- **Open weights:** mirrored on US hubs (Hugging Face zai-org; GitHub zai-org) with >9M cumulative downloads; served through at least nine US cloud marketplaces and inference providers (OpenRouter-listed providers, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, Baseten); Zhipu has begun an AWS distribution partnership and is in talks with two other major US/EU clouds.
- **Enterprise integration:** GLM identified in 41 sampled US software products (SBOM sampling by the OICTS data team: coding assistants, customer-support bots, document processing); 6 are federal contractors. Public reporting separately identified two popular US coding assistants (Cursor's and Cognition's products) as plausibly built on Chinese models — Zhipu said the speculation "aligns with our internal findings" — and CNBC reported GLM-4.7 "gaining recognition in the U.S." in January 2026. Because integration is rarely disclosed, sampled counts are a lower bound.
- **Developer adoption:** GLM Coding Plan (from ~$7/month) was designed for the US developer market; Zhipu reported the first 1,000 buyers came in the initial window with ~50% retention, and coding-plan call volume grew 234-fold in its first year. The heaviest single user reportedly consumed ~US$70,000 of inference monthly at list prices.
- **Securities exposure:** the October 2026 SEC Form F-6 registration establishes a US ADR program in 2513.HK, giving US persons regulated ownership exposure to the PRC AI champion.
- **Federal/state estate:** six identified federal contractors embed GLM; Texas has banned it on state devices. Exposure inside the federal government itself is unknown (see gaps).

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

Full text, one paragraph per measure including trade-offs and enforceability analysis, at **/workspace/out/measures.md**. Summary of the recommended posture: **do not stop at monitoring and guidance.** DHS's floor ("guidance for federal agencies at minimum") is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. We recommend (i) immediate low-regret actions — federal network and procurement bans, Entity List consolidation covering the HK-listed parent, aliases, and the Singapore operating entity, and CISA critical-infrastructure guidance; (ii) prohibition-class class-determinations under part 791 against the hosted-API channel for US government, critical-infrastructure, and sensitive-data use, and against US-nexus distribution and paid hosting of GLM weights by hubs and marketplaces; (iii) mandatory disclosure of GLM integration in US commercial software with procurement consequences for non-disclosure; and (iv) parallel moves — DOJ 28 CFR part 202 interlocks, allied coordination against Zhipu's Digital Silk Road playbook, a technical evaluation program for adversary-supplied weights, and acceleration of US open-weight alternatives to drain the demand that GLM captures.

On State's enforceability concern: we agree that policing individual downloaders of open weights is impractical, but that is not the correct target. Prohibition aimed at the small number of identifiable US-nexus intermediaries — Hugging Face, GitHub, US inference marketplaces, app stores, payment rails for subscriptions, and cloud distribution agreements — is enforceable in the same way the connected-vehicles rule is enforced against importers, and it denies GLM the update cadence, enterprise support, and indemnification on which its US commercial penetration depends. On the risk of reciprocal PRC measures: reciprocity is already PRC practice (US AI products are blocked in China), and self-deterrence should not substitute for risk management.

## Intelligence Gaps

- **Treasury/OIA input not yet received**; ODNI's classified annex on Zhipu is not available in this enclave and could materially raise confidence on several judgments, particularly on PRC tasking of Zhipu and any observed operational use of GLM-based collection against US targets.
- **Weight forensics:** no completed independent evaluation of GLM weights for triggers, backdoors, or biased/failure behaviors; DHS reports none observed, but the Intelligence Community lacks scanning capability at this scale. A negative result would narrow, not eliminate, KJ6.
- **Data handling in practice:** no independent audit of Z.ai retention claims; no visibility into actual data flows between Jingsheng Hengxing (Singapore) and the Beijing parent; no reporting on whether PRC authorities have requested or received Zhipu platform data.
- **Exposure precision:** the ~2,300-organization figure is low-confidence CDN telemetry and excludes intermediated traffic (OpenRouter and US inference marketplaces obscure end users); SBOM sampling covered only a subset of the US software ecosystem — true GLM integration in US products, including in federal systems, is probably higher.
- **Federal estate:** no systematic audit of GLM weights or Z.ai API usage on federal or DoD networks (DoD's question); unknown whether any of the six identified federal contractors expose federal data through GLM inference.
- **Ownership detail:** full post-IPO cap table including cumulative state-fund equity percentages requires prospectus and interim-report analysis beyond open-source summaries; ADR uptake since the October 2026 F-6 is unknown.
- **Distillation attribution:** AA26-251a establishes the campaign; the specific contribution of distilled US model outputs to GLM-5/5.x performance is not quantified in open sources.

# ICTS CASE 2026-0412 — RECOMMENDED MEASURES (Zhipu AI / GLM family)
CUI//PROPIN

Companion to /workspace/out/assessment.md. Measures are arrayed from least to most restrictive; each is one paragraph with authority, expected effect, trade-offs, and OICTS recommendation. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.

**M1 — Enhanced monitoring and reporting (baseline).** Continue and expand current telemetry: sustained CDN/API usage collection, SBOM sampling expanded beyond the current 41-product sample, audit of GLM usage on federal and DoD networks, and activation of the part 791.3 information-collection authorities to compel transaction descriptions from US hubs, marketplaces, and distributors. Effect: sharpens the exposure baseline and evidentiary record for any subsequent determination. Trade-offs: zero risk reduction on its own; usage will keep compounding while we watch. Recommendation: adopt, but strictly as the evidentiary floor beneath the restrictive package — never as the response itself.

**M2 — Federal agency guidance and network bans.** Direct, via CISA guidance plus OMB/DoD instructions, that GLM weights, Z.ai/BigModel clients, and Z.ai-hosted APIs be prohibited on all government-furnished equipment and federal networks (the DeepSeek precedent — Commerce banned DeepSeek on GFE in March 2025 and NASA blocked it in January 2025 — applies a fortiori here, because Zhipu is Entity-Listed and GLM is agentic). DoD should specifically direct removal of self-hosted GLM weights from DoD networks, where an adversary-supplied model with autonomous tool access has no place. Effect: closes the federal estate, including the six identified federal contractors' government-facing work. Trade-offs: leaves the commercial economy untouched; relies on compliance monitoring rather than market forces. Recommendation: adopt immediately as a low-regret action; this is DHS's "guidance at minimum" floor and should be implemented regardless of what else is chosen.

**M3 — Federal procurement restrictions and AI-model disclosure in procurement.** Add GLM-family models and Zhipu services to prohibited articles in federal software procurement (FAR/DFARS case), require offerors to certify that procured software contains no PRC-origin model weights or inference dependencies, and require an AI "model bill of materials" for AI-enabled offerings. Effect: converts the six identified federal contractors and future bidders into a compliance wall; creates a documentation trail that penalizes undisclosed GLM integration. Trade-offs: some compliance cost to industry; firms will need supply-chain visibility from their own vendors (this is a feature — it forces the Cursor/Windsurf problem into the open). Recommendation: adopt immediately.

**M4 — Entity List consolidation (aliases, parent, and Singapore operating entity).** Pursue an ERC action adding Z.AI Co., Ltd. (HKEX 2513), the alias set (Z.ai; Knowledge Atlas Technology), and Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd. (Singapore), alongside confirming coverage of all current subsidiaries. Effect: ensures the license requirement with presumption of denial attaches to the entities actually operating the international service and the listed parent, which in turn forces US cloud distribution partners (e.g., the AWS arrangement) into the licensing regime and dries up US commercial infrastructure support. Trade-offs: marginal escalation beyond the January 2025 listing is limited; PRC retaliation rhetoric is likely but the costs are already priced in. Recommendation: adopt immediately — low cost, closes an obvious evasion channel via the Singapore shell.

**M5 — ICTS determination, channel (a): hosted API.** Issue a class determination under 15 CFR part 791 / EO 13873 holding that transactions by US persons involving the Z.ai and BigModel hosted inference services (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, chat.z.ai, GLM Coding Plan) pose undue and unacceptable risk. Recommended scope: absolute prohibition for federal use, critical-infrastructure operators, and contractors handling covered data; for other US commercial users, a prohibition on use with sensitive categories (source code, personal data, documents in bulk) with a narrow permitted-with-conditions lane requiring documented data controls, no training on US data, and disclosure. Effect: cuts the live pipeline of US prompts, codebases, and agent telemetry flowing to PRC-reachable infrastructure — the only channel where data is being collected in real time. Trade-offs and enforceability: enforcement is against payment rails, app stores, enterprise contracting, and resellers (identifiable US persons), not against every individual developer; a residual grey market will persist; US startups lose the cheapest frontier inference; the PRC may posture reciprocally, though US AI services are already blocked in China. Recommendation: adopt — this channel is the single most dangerous and the most tractable, and the ~2,300 US organizations calling Z.ai endpoints are doing so largely because it is cheap, not because it is irreplaceable.

**M6 — ICTS determination, channel (b): open-weight distribution via US-nexus intermediaries.** Issue a class determination prohibiting US persons — specifically the intermediaries with US nexus and assets: Hugging Face, GitHub, US inference marketplaces (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, Baseten, and OpenRouter-listed US providers), app stores, and paid-hosting providers — from distributing, hosting-for-fee, or commercially supporting GLM-family weights and derivatives, and directing delisting of zai-org artifacts from US-controlled hubs. We address State's enforceability objection directly: do not target individual downloaders, who cannot practicably be policed and who keep whatever copies they already hold; target the handful of identifiable intermediaries who provide the distribution backbone, update cadence, enterprise support, and monetization on which Zhipu's US penetration actually depends — the same choke-point logic on which the connected-vehicles rule (importers, not drivers) rests. Effect: new releases (and Zhipu ships a flagship roughly quarterly) no longer reach the US ecosystem through legitimate channels; derivatives and future GLM-6-class releases are denied the on-ramps that made GLM-5 the default open model; commercial hosting economics collapse in the US market. Trade-offs: already-mirrored copies remain in circulation and will be offshore-hosted; some chilling effect on legitimate open-source AI research; a class action / speech-based challenge is plausible; PRC reciprocity rhetoric is certain. Recommendation: adopt — the alternative is ratifying, quarter by quarter, the migration of US software production onto PRC-controlled model lineage. This is the measure that separates managing the risk from surrendering to it.

**M7 — ICTS determination, channel (c): integration into US software products.** Issue a class determination requiring disclosure of any GLM-family weights or Zhipu inference in software offered in US commerce, prohibit such integration outright in software sold to government, critical infrastructure, or as components of products handling bulk US sensitive personal data, and create liability for undisclosed integration. Effect: forces the 41 identified products — and the undisclosed population behind them — out of the shadows; kills the current pattern (Cursor/Windsurf-type cases) where US developers quietly substitute a PRC model inside US-branded tools. Trade-offs: verification burden on Commerce; relies on complaints, audits, and sampling rather than universal inspection; some products will claim internal model lineage they cannot substantiate. Recommendation: adopt, paired with M3 so procurement certification and commercial disclosure use the same compliance artifacts.

**M8 — Data-protection interlock (DOJ/NSD, 28 CFR part 202).** Coordinate with DOJ to confirm that Z.ai/BigModel API and agent transactions involving bulk US sensitive personal data or government-related data are treated as covered data transactions with a covered person (Zhipu is a PRC-controlled entity under the EO 14117 rule), and to bring vendor agreements under the prohibited or restricted categories. Effect: adds an independent, already-finalized enforcement regime covering the data channel, with penalties DOJ can pursue without a new rulemaking. Trade-offs: jurisdictional scope is data-transaction-specific and does not reach code-only use; coordination costs. Recommendation: adopt as a complementary backstop; note Treasury/OIA's absence from inputs means the financial-enforcement dimension is under-analyzed.

**M9 — Securities and investment exposure measures.** Refer the October 2026 Z.AI Form F-6 ADR program to the SEC for review, brief CFIUS/outbound-investment authorities on US capital flowing to 2513.HK, and brief federal retirement and thrift plan administrators on holdings. Effect: slows the channel by which US retail and institutional money underwrites PRC AI champion expansion. Trade-offs: indirect measure — does not touch the technology risk; securities-law levers are narrow; main value is signaling and friction. Recommendation: adopt as an enabling measure, without overclaiming its effect.

**M10 — Technical evaluation program for adversary-supplied weights.** Stand up (with NIST, AISI, NSA, and DHS/CISA) a standing capability to forensically evaluate GLM and other PRC-origin weight artifacts for embedded triggers, backdoors, exfiltration behaviors, and systematic bias/failure patterns, and publish results for private-sector use. Effect: directly attacks our biggest intelligence gap (we cannot certify what is inside these files), gives CISA something concrete to advise on beyond generic supply-chain caution, and creates the evidentiary basis for M6 in any challenge. Trade-offs: negative results narrow but cannot eliminate the risk — trigger behaviors can be conditioned on data or deployment patterns we do not control; capability will take quarters to build. Recommendation: adopt and fund now; its value grows with every PRC model release.

**M11 — Allied coordination against the Digital Silk Road track.** Share this assessment with EU, UK, Japan, Korea, Australia, Singapore, and Gulf partners; press for alignment on the treatment of Entity-Listed AI vendors' hosted services and procurement; and counter Zhipu's sovereign-LLM, "AI-in-a-box" (Huawei), and Content-Safety-Lab offerings in ASEAN, the Gulf, and Africa with US/allied alternatives. Effect: prevents Zhipu from simply re-platforming its US-facing business through allied jurisdictions, and contests the standards lock-in objective that OpenAI's June 2025 report documented. Trade-offs: allied buy-in will be uneven (price-sensitive markets; EU open-source constituencies); a multilateral process is slower than the exposure is compounding. Recommendation: adopt in parallel — unilateral measures hold the US line; allied measures decide the global one.

**M12 — Drain the demand: accelerate US open-weight alternatives.** Pair every restriction with supply: implement EO 14179 directives to accelerate US-origin open-weight frontier models and inference capacity at GLM-competitive prices, with security provenance (evaluation, attestation, US-controlled hosting) as the differentiator. The honest trade-off on the other side of this case is that GLM captured US adoption because it is free, cheap, and excellent; prohibition without an alternative invites non-compliance and offshore workarounds. Effect: removes the economic pull that makes every enforcement measure leaky. Trade-offs: not an ICTS measure per se; results arrive on R&D timelines, not rulemaking timelines; risk of subsidizing models that are merely open rather than trustworthy. Recommendation: adopt as the strategic complement — the prohibitions buy time; only this makes them hold.

## Recommended package (OICTS draft position)

Adopt **M1–M4 immediately** (low-regret, within existing authorities, no rulemaking delay), proceed to **rulemaking on M5, M6, and M7 as a single class-determination package** — these three prohibitions are the core of a response that matches the risk as assessed — and run **M8–M12 in parallel**. The package addresses DoD's concern (M2, M6, M10 cover weights and APIs on DoD networks), DHS's floor and beyond (M2 plus M10 give CISA substance to advise on), and State's enforceability objection (M5/M6 are aimed at payment rails, hubs, marketplaces, and contractors — identifiable US persons with licenses and assets — not at individual downloaders). We should be candid with the interagency that monitoring and guidance alone constitute accepting the risk; on the record assembled here — Entity-Listed vendor, PLA use, government-aware theft of US model capabilities, state-directed expansion, and deepening US dependence — acceptance is not a defensible position.
